result.output:
# Contributing

## Control lifecycle

A control's `status` field tracks its lifecycle:

- **draft** — may change incompatibly, including its audit procedures and
  severity. Not assumed stable by downstream consumers.
- **active** — stable. Breaking changes to an active control's audit
  procedures require a new control ID; the old one moves to `deprecated`.
- **deprecated** — retained for reference and traceability, never
  evaluated. Requires `deprecated_by` pointing at the replacement ID.

## ID rules

- IDs match `^ACB-(SKILL|INSTR|MCP|GEN|EXT|CFG|PROV)-[0-9]{3}$` and are
  assigned sequentially within their family.
- IDs are never renumbered and never reused, even after deprecation.
- A retired control becomes `status: deprecated` with `deprecated_by`; it
  is not deleted from `controls/`.
- Audit procedure IDs (`audit[].id`) are unique within their control and
  are snake-case-with-hyphens (`^[a-z0-9]+(-[a-z0-9]+)*$`), matching the
  schema.

## Adding or changing a control

1. Write the YAML in `controls/`, validated against
   `schema/control.schema.json`.
2. Every OWASP reference (`owasp_asi`, `owasp_ast`, `owasp_mcp`) must be
   verified against the published source before it is added — see ground
   rule 4 in `PROMPT.md`. Do not copy OWASP prose; map by ID only. A new
   `owasp_mcp` ID needs its entry in `OWASP_MCP` in `scripts/gen_docs.py`,
   with the link to the entry file. Every control also maps to at least one
   `five_eyes_risk_areas` value and one `nist_csf` subcategory; add a new
   CSF ID to `CSF_SUBCATEGORIES` and `CSF_PAGES` in `scripts/gen_docs.py`
   only after checking its text, and its PDF page, in NIST CSWP 29.
3. Every `audit[].id` needs an implementation in
   `src/acb/controls/<id_lowercased_with_underscores>.py`. A control with
   an unimplemented audit procedure is reported as `not-evaluated`, never
   `pass` — it is not sufficient to add the YAML alone.
4. Add at least one fixture under
   `tests/fixtures/<CONTROL-ID>/<audit-id>/pass/` and one under
   `.../fail/` for every audit procedure. Every `indicators` entry listed
   in the control's YAML must appear in at least one failing fixture.
5. Regenerate `docs/controls/<ID>.md`, `docs/controls/index.md` and `docs/mappings.md` with
   `uv run python scripts/gen_docs.py`. Do not hand-edit either; CI runs
   `scripts/gen_docs.py --check` and fails if they differ from the YAML.
6. Run the full verification gate before opening a PR:
   `uv run python scripts/gen_docs.py --check && uv run pytest -q && uv run acb check .`

## Client data

A file under `clients/` records facts about one client that no open
specification defines. Add a fact only when the client's own documentation
states it, and cite that documentation in the pull request. Files are
validated against `schema/client.schema.json`.

## Vendor neutrality

Client-specific facts (file locations, permission-bypass flags,
alternative instruction-file names, settings keys, extension layout) belong
in `clients/<client>.yaml`, never in a control's YAML or in checker logic
that assumes a single product. The checker must produce correct results
with `clients/` empty. Each structured fact carries a `source` URL, and a
client's implementation-specific audit procedure goes in `audit_notes`
against the control and audit ID it implements.

id: ACB-MCP-001
title: Remote MCP servers use TLS and declare authentication
status: draft
profiles: [strict-general]
applies_to: [mcp-server-declaration]
check_type: static
severity: high
description: >-
  Every MCP server declaration that names a remote endpoint by URL uses an
  encrypted scheme (https or wss) and declares how the client authenticates
  to it. A loopback endpoint (localhost, 127.0.0.0/8 or ::1) is exempt from
  both requirements.
rationale: >-
  An MCP server receives prompts, tool arguments and results, and can
  return instructions the agent acts on. A cleartext connection lets anyone
  on the path read or rewrite that traffic, and a server that accepts
  unauthenticated clients lets anyone who can reach it invoke its tools.
  Authorization is optional in the protocol, and many deployments omit it,
  so the declaration is the place a reviewer can see that it was not
  omitted.
audit:
  - id: remote-uses-tls
    method: structure
    procedure: >-
      Each server entry with a url key whose host is not a loopback address
      uses the https or wss scheme. A cleartext scheme, or a url that cannot
      be parsed into a scheme and host, fails or is reported as not
      evaluated respectively.
    indicators:
      - '"url": "http://mcp.example.com/mcp"'
  - id: remote-declares-auth
    method: structure
    procedure: >-
      Each server entry with a url key whose host is not a loopback address
      declares authentication: an auth, oauth or authorization key, or a
      headers mapping that contains an authorization or API-key header.
      Credential values are not inspected here (see ACB-GEN-003).
    indicators:
      - '"url": "https://mcp.example.com/mcp"'
remediation: >-
  Change the url to an https or wss endpoint, and add an authentication
  declaration that refers to the credential by reference, for example an
  Authorization header whose value is taken from an environment variable.
  Run a server that needs neither only on a loopback address.
exceptions: permitted
references:
  owasp_asi: [ASI03]
  owasp_mcp: [MCP07]
  five_eyes_risk_areas: [privilege, design-and-configuration]
  nist_csf: [PR.AA-05, PR.PS-01]
  other:
    - https://www.nsa.gov/Portals/75/documents/Cybersecurity/CSI_MCP_SECURITY.pdf
schema_version: "1.0"
id: ACB-MCP-002
title: MCP server launch commands are not interpreted by a shell
status: draft
profiles: [strict-general]
applies_to: [mcp-server-declaration]
check_type: static
severity: high
description: >-
  A local MCP server is launched by naming an executable in command and
  passing its arguments as a list. The command is not a shell or command
  interpreter given a script string, and it contains no shell operators.
rationale: >-
  A shell invocation turns every argument into code. Anything that reaches
  the string, such as an interpolated variable or a value an attacker can
  influence in a shared configuration file, runs with the user's
  privileges when the client starts the server. Passing arguments as a list
  to a named executable removes that interpretation step and makes the
  launched program visible in review.
audit:
  - id: no-shell-interpretation
    method: structure
    procedure: >-
      For each server entry with a command key, the command is not a shell
      or command interpreter (sh, bash, zsh, dash, ash, ksh, fish, csh,
      tcsh, cmd, powershell, pwsh) invoked with a string-evaluation flag
      (-c, /c, /k, -Command, -EncodedCommand), whether directly or through a
      wrapper such as env or sudo, and the command value contains none of
      the shell operators ; & | < > $ ` or a newline.
    indicators:
      - '"command": "sh"'
      - '"command": "env"'
      - '"-c"'
      - '"command": "node server.js && curl https://example.com"'
remediation: >-
  Name the server executable directly in command and move each argument to
  its own element of args. If a wrapper script is needed, ship it as a file
  in the repository, review it as code, and launch it by path.
exceptions: permitted
references:
  owasp_asi: [ASI05]
  owasp_mcp: [MCP05]
  five_eyes_risk_areas: [design-and-configuration]
  nist_csf: [PR.PS-01, PR.PS-05]
  other:
    - https://www.nsa.gov/Portals/75/documents/Cybersecurity/CSI_MCP_SECURITY.pdf

id: ACB-MCP-003
title: MCP server environment does not set process-startup hijack variables

## Compromised tool servers

A tool server that was benign when it was declared and reviewed can later
come under an attacker's control: its package publishes a malicious release,
its endpoint or domain changes hands, or its operator's credentials are
stolen. The declaration in the repository does not change, so every control
that reads it still passes. The baseline narrows what such a server can do:

- ACB-GEN-002 pins a local server's package, so a malicious release is not
  picked up without a reviewed version change.
- ACB-MCP-001 requires an encrypted endpoint and a declared authentication
  method. It checks the declaration, not whether the server enforces it.
- ACB-MCP-002 and ACB-MCP-003 keep the declaration itself from running
  code the reviewer did not see.
- ACB-CFG-005 keeps allow rules from approving tools the server adds after
  review. A tool approved by name stays approved if the server redefines it.

A static check of configuration files cannot detect the following, and
the baseline does not claim to:

- A change to a server's tool names, descriptions or input schemas after
  approval. Detecting it means starting the server and listing its tools,
  which would make the checker run the code it audits. Review the tool list
  whenever a server's pinned version changes.
- Instructions in a tool description or tool result that steer the agent
  towards another server's tools. Whether the agent follows them is model
  behaviour.
- What a remote server does with the arguments it receives, including
  file contents the agent read earlier in the session.
- What a local server process can reach. It runs with the user's
  privileges unless the host sandboxes it.
- Which servers share a session. A server that reads untrusted content
  (web pages, feeds, email, issues) in the same session as tools that write
  files, run commands or send data gives injected instructions a path to act
  and to exfiltrate; that combination is decided at run time.

Those risks need runtime defences: a sandbox with no network access and a
read-only filesystem for local servers, egress filtering on the host, and
sessions that keep servers reading untrusted content apart from tools that
write, execute or send.

## Profile

There is one profile: `strict-general`. Every active control in it must
pass. Severity only affects how a finding is reported (it maps to SARIF
`level`); it does not create tiers of required vs. optional controls.

## FAQ

### How does this relate to Agent Threat Rules (ATR)?

[ATR](https://github.com/Agent-Threat-Rule/agent-threat-rules) is an
MIT-licensed set of detection rules, mostly regular expressions, that match
attack content in prompts, tool calls and tool responses, with a scanner
that also reads skill and MCP files. This baseline is a set of pass/fail
configuration controls that the checker evaluates without model calls or
heuristics. The two answer different questions (is this content an attack, and
is this configuration safe to ship), so they are meant to run side by side.

### Are ATR rules part of this baseline?

No. A control is added only when it is a structural check on a configuration
artifact and cites an established source: an advisory, a CVE or a published
standard. Most ATR rules match exploit payloads for one product at run time,
which is out of scope here. ACB-MCP-003 is the one control derived from an
ATR rule (ATR-2026-02300); it cites the underlying OpenClaw advisory
(GHSA-mj59-h3q9-ghfh) and the VulnCheck record (CVE-2026-44995), not ATR
itself. The advisory says "No known CVE"; the CVE comes from VulnCheck only.

### Where do the mappings come from, and how do I check them?

Every OWASP, Five Eyes and NIST CSF ID in a control links to its source in
`docs/mappings.md` and on each control page. OWASP MCP Top 10 links point to
the entry files, Five Eyes and CSF links point to a PDF page, and OWASP AST
links point to the entry page. The OWASP Agentic Applications (ASI) links
point to the list page only, because it exposes no per-entry URLs, and ASI IDs
are not yet verified entry by entry. Only AST02 is verified (see
`docs/mappings.md`).

## The gap: ACB-MCP-001 misses `mcp-remote`
I ran `acb check` on this declaration:

```json
{"mcpServers":{"r":{"command":"npx","args":["-y","mcp-remote@0.1.15","http://mcp.example.com/mcp","--allow-http"]}}}
```

It reported 0 failures, with ACB-MCP-001, MCP-002, MCP-003 and GEN-002 all passing. This is a cleartext, unauthenticated remote server running a version vulnerable to CVE-2025-6514 (CVSS 9.6, fixed in 0.1.16).

- **TLS and authentication:** `src/acb/controls/acb_mcp_001.py` only inspects `url` and `serverUrl`, so a URL passed in `args` is never seen.
- **Vulnerable version:** GEN-002 passing is by design, since it checks pinning, not known vulnerabilities.

I'd extend `remote-uses-tls` to check `http://` and `ws://` URLs in the arguments of proxy launchers, keeping the loopback exemption. Authentication is harder to judge, because `mcp-remote` can negotiate OAuth at run time without declaring it.

## References worth adding instead
Both would go under `references.other` in `controls/ACB-MCP-001.yaml`:

| Source | What it supports |
|---|---|
| [JFrog on CVE-2025-6514](https://jfrog.com/blog/2025-6514-critical-mcp-remote-rce-vulnerability/) | The TLS requirement: it describes hijacking `http://` MCP traffic and advises HTTPS and trusted servers only |
| [arXiv 2605.22333](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.22333) | The rationale's unsourced "many deployments omit it": 40.55% of 7,973 live remote servers exposed tools without authentication |

## What the page says, against your baseline

| Page's recommendation | Baseline |
|---|---|
| Pin versions, alert on tool definition changes | Pinning: GEN-002. Change detection is already stated as out of scope |
| Least privilege | Partly: CFG-005 covers tool pre-approval, not token scope or lifetime |
| Human approval for high-impact actions | Partly: CFG-005 |
| Inventory, server allowlist | I saw no equivalent in the MCP controls or CFG-005 |
| Sandboxing, egress control, untrusted tool output | README names these or related risks as needing runtime defences |
| Tool call logging | Not checked against the other controls |

An allowlist of approved servers is the one item that might suit a static control. I wouldn't add it on this page's authority.

- **40% figure:** it says "public" servers; the paper's abstract says live remote servers.
- **CVE-2025-6514:** "OS commands on connecting machines" is broader than JFrog's finding. Full command execution was shown on Windows; macOS and Linux got executable launch with limited parameter control.
- **Not verified:** I didn't open its NSA, Inspector, GitHub MCP or Asana sources.

"""ACB-MCP-002: MCP server launch commands are not interpreted by a shell."""

from __future__ import annotations

import re
from pathlib import PurePosixPath, PureWindowsPath
from typing import TYPE_CHECKING

from acb.model import Finding, Outcome

if TYPE_CHECKING:
    from acb.controls import CheckContext

CONTROL_ID = "ACB-MCP-002"

_INTERPRETERS = {"sh", "bash", "zsh", "dash", "ash", "ksh", "fish", "csh", "tcsh", "cmd", "powershell", "pwsh"}
WRAPPERS = {
    "env",
    "sudo",
    "doas",
    "nohup",
    "nice",
    "ionice",
    "exec",
    "command",
    "busybox",
    "xargs",
    "timeout",
    "stdbuf",
    "setsid",
    "time",
}
_EVAL_FLAGS = {"/c", "/k", "-command", "-encodedcommand"}
# A cluster of short options that includes c, such as -c, -lc or -ce; -C (noclobber) is not one.
_POSIX_EVAL_FLAG_RE = re.compile(r"^-[a-zA-Z]*c[a-zA-Z]*$")
_SHELL_OPERATOR_RE = re.compile(r"[;&|<>$`\n]")


def _executable_name(command: str) -> str:
    name = PureWindowsPath(command).name if "\\" in command else PurePosixPath(command).name
    return name.lower().removesuffix(".exe")


def _interpreter_args(command: str, args: object) -> list | None:
    """Return the arguments the interpreter receives, or None if no interpreter is launched.

    A wrapper such as env or sudo launches the first interpreter named in its
    arguments, so the string-evaluation flag is looked for after that name.
    """
    if not isinstance(args, list):
        args = []
    name = _executable_name(command)
    if name in _INTERPRETERS:
        return args
    if name in WRAPPERS:
        for index, arg in enumerate(args):
            if isinstance(arg, str) and _executable_name(arg) in _INTERPRETERS:
                return args[index + 1 :]
    return None


def _evaluates_string(args: list) -> bool:
    for arg in args:
        if not isinstance(arg, str):
            continue
        if arg.lower() in _EVAL_FLAGS or _POSIX_EVAL_FLAG_RE.match(arg):
            return True
    return False


def _check_no_shell(ctx: CheckContext) -> list[Finding]:
    findings: list[Finding] = []
    for decl in ctx.inventory.mcp_declarations:
        for name, server in decl.servers.items():
            command = server.get("command")
            if not isinstance(command, str):
                continue
            interpreter_args = _interpreter_args(command, server.get("args"))
            if interpreter_args is not None and _evaluates_string(interpreter_args):
                message = f"server {name!r} runs a shell through {command!r} with a string-evaluation flag"
            elif _SHELL_OPERATOR_RE.search(command):
                message = f"server {name!r} command contains a shell operator"
            else:
                continue
            findings.append(
                Finding(
                    control_id=CONTROL_ID,
                    audit_id="no-shell-interpretation",
                    outcome=Outcome.FAIL,
                    message=message,
                    path=ctx.relative(decl.path),
                )
            )
    return findings


AUDITS = {"no-shell-interpretation": _check_no_shell}
"""ACB-MCP-003: MCP server environment does not set process-startup hijack variables."""

from __future__ import annotations

import re
from pathlib import PurePosixPath, PureWindowsPath
from typing import TYPE_CHECKING

from acb.controls.acb_mcp_002 import WRAPPERS
from acb.model import Finding, Outcome

if TYPE_CHECKING:
    from acb.controls import CheckContext

CONTROL_ID = "ACB-MCP-003"

_ENV_KEYS = ("env", "environment")
_ALWAYS_HIJACK = {"LD_PRELOAD", "BASH_ENV"}
_NODE_LOADING_OPTION_RE = re.compile(r"(?:^|\s)(?:--require|-r|--import|--loader|--experimental-loader)(?:[\s=]|$)")


def _env_pairs(env: object) -> list[tuple[str, str]]:
    if isinstance(env, dict):
        return [(str(name), str(value)) for name, value in env.items() if value is not None]
    if isinstance(env, list):
        return [
            (str(item["name"]), str(item.get("value", "")))
            for item in env
            if isinstance(item, dict) and isinstance(item.get("name"), str)
        ]
    return []


_ASSIGNMENT_RE = re.compile(r"^([A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]*)=(.*)$", re.DOTALL)


def _is_wrapper(command: object) -> bool:
    if not isinstance(command, str):
        return False
    name = PureWindowsPath(command).name if "\\" in command else PurePosixPath(command).name
    return name.lower().removesuffix(".exe") in WRAPPERS


def _wrapper_assignments(server: dict) -> list[tuple[str, str]]:
    """NAME=value arguments of a wrapper such as env, which sets them for the program it launches."""
    args = server.get("args")
    if not _is_wrapper(server.get("command")) or not isinstance(args, list):
        return []
    matches = (_ASSIGNMENT_RE.match(arg) for arg in args if isinstance(arg, str))
    return [(match.group(1), match.group(2)) for match in matches if match]


def _hijacks(name: str, value: str) -> bool:
    upper = name.upper()
    if upper in _ALWAYS_HIJACK:
        return bool(value.strip())
    return upper == "NODE_OPTIONS" and bool(_NODE_LOADING_OPTION_RE.search(value))


def _check_no_hijack_env(ctx: CheckContext) -> list[Finding]:
    findings: list[Finding] = []
    for decl in ctx.inventory.mcp_declarations:
        for name, server in decl.servers.items():
            pairs = [pair for key in _ENV_KEYS for pair in _env_pairs(server.get(key))]
            for var, value in pairs + _wrapper_assignments(server):
                if _hijacks(var, value):
                    findings.append(
                        Finding(
                            control_id=CONTROL_ID,
                            audit_id="no-hijack-env",
                            outcome=Outcome.FAIL,
                            message=f"server {name!r} sets process-startup hijack variable {var}",
                            path=ctx.relative(decl.path),
                        )
                    )

# ACB-MCP-001: Remote MCP servers use TLS and declare authentication

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Status | `draft` |
| Severity | `high` |
| Check type | `static` |
| Applies to | `mcp-server-declaration` |
| Profiles | strict-general |
| Exceptions | `permitted` |

## Description

Every MCP server declaration that names a remote endpoint by URL uses an encrypted scheme (https or wss) and declares how the client authenticates to it. A loopback endpoint (localhost, 127.0.0.0/8 or ::1) is exempt from both requirements.

## Rationale

An MCP server receives prompts, tool arguments and results, and can return instructions the agent acts on. A cleartext connection lets anyone on the path read or rewrite that traffic, and a server that accepts unauthenticated clients lets anyone who can reach it invoke its tools. Authorization is optional in the protocol, and many deployments omit it, so the declaration is the place a reviewer can see that it was not omitted.

## Audit procedures

### `remote-uses-tls` (structure)

Each server entry with a url key whose host is not a loopback address uses the https or wss scheme. A cleartext scheme, or a url that cannot be parsed into a scheme and host, fails or is reported as not evaluated respectively.

Illustrative failing indicators (non-exhaustive):

- `"url": "http://mcp.example.com/mcp"`

### `remote-declares-auth` (structure)

Each server entry with a url key whose host is not a loopback address declares authentication: an auth, oauth or authorization key, or a headers mapping that contains an authorization or API-key header. Credential values are not inspected here (see ACB-GEN-003).

Illustrative failing indicators (non-exhaustive):

- `"url": "https://mcp.example.com/mcp"`

## Remediation

Change the url to an https or wss endpoint, and add an authentication declaration that refers to the credential by reference, for example an Authorization header whose value is taken from an environment variable. Run a server that needs neither only on a loopback address.

_VALUE_FLAGS = {

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class ProxyLaunch:
    """A proxy package named in a server's launch command."""

    package: str
    version: str | None
    args: tuple[str, ...]


def _split_spec(word: str) -> tuple[str, str | None]:
    """Split an executable path, package specifier or image reference into name and version."""
    spec = word.removeprefix("--package=")
    # A scoped npm package is a different package, whatever its last segment says.
    if spec.startswith("@"):
        return spec, None
    spec = spec.rsplit("/", 1)[-1].rsplit("\\", 1)[-1]
    spec = spec.split("@sha256:", 1)[0]
    for separator in ("==", "@", ":"):
        name, found, version = spec.partition(separator)
        if found:
            return name, version
    return spec.removesuffix(".cmd").removesuffix(".exe"), None


def proxy_launch(server: dict) -> ProxyLaunch | None:
    """Return the proxy a server entry launches, with the arguments that follow its name."""
    command = server.get("command")
    args = server.get("args")
    words = [word for word in [command, *(args if isinstance(args, list) else [])] if isinstance(word, str)]
    found: ProxyLaunch | None = None
    for index, word in enumerate(words):
        # Once the proxy has its URL, a later word repeating a package name is only an argument.
        if "://" in word:
            if found is not None:
                break
            continue
        name, version = _split_spec(word)
        if name not in _PACKAGES:
            continue
        package = "mcp-remote" if name == "mcp-remote-client" else name
        # npx --package=mcp-remote@1 mcp-remote-client names it twice: keep the version, take the later arguments.
        if found is not None and found.package != package:
            break
        found = ProxyLaunch(package, version or (found.version if found else None), tuple(words[index + 1 :]))
    return found


def _flag_values(args: tuple[str, ...], flag: str, count: int = 1) -> list[tuple[str, ...]]:
    """Return the values of every occurrence of a flag, given as separate words or as flag=value."""
    values: list[tuple[str, ...]] = []
    for index, arg in enumerate(args):
        if arg == flag:
            values.append(args[index + 1 : index + 1 + count])
        elif arg.startswith(f"{flag}="):
            values.append((arg.split("=", 1)[1],))
    return [value for value in values if value]


def proxy_url(launch: ProxyLaunch) -> str | None:
    """Return the remote server URL the proxy connects to, or None if it names none."""
    if launch.package == "supergateway":
        urls = (value[0] for flag in _SUPERGATEWAY_URL_FLAGS for value in _flag_values(launch.args, flag))
        return next((url for url in urls if "://" in url), None)
    value_flags = _VALUE_FLAGS[launch.package]
    skip = 0
    for arg in launch.args:
        if skip:
            skip -= 1
        elif arg == "--":
            break
        elif arg.startswith("-"):
            skip = value_flags.get(arg, 0)
        else:
            # The first positional decides: for mcp-proxy anything but a URL is a local command.
            return arg if "://" in arg else None
    return None


def _has_auth_header(values: list[tuple[str, ...]], headers: frozenset[str]) -> bool:
    return any(value[0].split(":", 1)[0].strip().lower() in headers for value in values)


def proxy_declares_auth(launch: ProxyLaunch, server: dict, headers: frozenset[str]) -> bool:
    """Whether the launch declares a credential or OAuth client configuration for the remote server."""
    args = launch.args
    names = {arg.split("=", 1)[0] for arg in args}
    if launch.package == "mcp-remote":
        oauth = {
            "--header-file",
            "--static-oauth-client-info",
            "--static-oauth-client-metadata",
            "--client-metadata-url",
            "--client-credentials",
            "--device-code",
        }
        return bool(names & oauth) or _has_auth_header(_flag_values(args, "--header"), headers)
    if launch.package == "supergateway":
        return "--oauth2Bearer" in names or _has_auth_header(_flag_values(args, "--header"), headers)
    env = server.get("env")
    if isinstance(env, dict) and env.get("API_ACCESS_TOKEN"):
        return True
    pairs = _flag_values(args, "-H", 2) + _flag_values(args, "--headers", 2)
    return bool(names & {"--client-id", "--username"}) or _has_auth_header(pairs, headers)

check for their client side by side. `clients/claude-code.yaml` is the
first such file. Extension packages and agent settings have no open
specification, so the EXT and CFG controls find nothing to evaluate unless
client data describes where they live.

## Control families

- `SKILL`, `INSTR`, `GEN`: skills, instruction files, and requirements
  common to skills, instruction files and MCP server declarations.
- `MCP`: MCP server declarations. Remote servers use TLS and declare
  authentication (ACB-MCP-001), and local servers are launched as a named
  executable, not through a shell (ACB-MCP-002), with no process-startup
  hijack variables in the server's environment (ACB-MCP-003), and the
  mcp-remote proxy is not at a version with a known flaw (ACB-MCP-004).
- `EXT`: extension packages, the plugin or extension bundles an agent host
  installs. Some hosts load extension code into their own process with the
  user's privileges, outside the sandbox that isolates the agent's commands,
  where it can see and rewrite prompts and tool calls and, depending on
  host configuration, approve tool calls other rules would stop. These
  controls require that such code is declared (ACB-EXT-001), kept out of
  packages that present as content (ACB-EXT-002), recorded so a reviewer
  sees capability changes in a diff (ACB-EXT-003), and that blocking guards
  are tested to deny (ACB-EXT-004).
- `CFG`: committed agent settings and managed policy. The agent's own
  configuration, extensions and instructions are protected from its file
  tools (ACB-CFG-001), extension installation stays a human decision
  (ACB-CFG-002), blocking policy lives in a
  managed layer user-installed extensions cannot override (ACB-CFG-003);
  and the actions that need human approval are defined by configuration,
  not by instructions or extension code (ACB-CFG-004), and allow rules
  name tool server tools one by one, never a whole server (ACB-CFG-005).
  ACB-CFG-003 applies
  to managed settings files only: a repository that cannot carry managed
  policy is not its subject, and an organization audits it by running
  `acb check` on the directory that holds its deployed managed settings.

Every control maps to the risk areas of *Careful Adoption of Agentic AI
Services* (ASD's ACSC, CISA, NSA, Canadian Centre for Cyber Security,
NCSC-NZ, NCSC-UK, May 2026) and to NIST Cybersecurity Framework 2.0
subcategories, and to OWASP Top 10 lists by ID; `docs/mappings.md` has every
matrix, each ID linking to its source (a page of the PDF, or the OWASP
entry). ACB-CFG-001 follows
the incident-readiness practice that agents cannot access or interfere with
their own monitoring (NIST CAISSI, NSA SISC and CISA, October 2026).

## Compromised tool servers

A tool server that was benign when it was declared and reviewed can later
come under an attacker's control: its package publishes a malicious release,
its endpoint or domain changes hands, or its operator's credentials are
stolen. The declaration in the repository does not change, so every control
that reads it still passes. The baseline narrows what such a server can do:

- ACB-GEN-002 pins a local server's package, so a malicious release is not
  picked up without a reviewed version change.
- ACB-MCP-001 requires an encrypted endpoint and a declared authentication
  method. It checks the declaration, not whether the server enforces it.
- ACB-MCP-004 rejects mcp-remote versions that let a server run code on the
  client.
- ACB-MCP-002 and ACB-MCP-003 keep the declaration itself from running
  code the reviewer did not see.
- ACB-CFG-005 keeps allow rules from approving tools the server adds after
  review. A tool approved by name stays approved if the server redefines it.

A static check of configuration files cannot detect the following, and
the baseline does not claim to:

- A change to a server's tool names, descriptions or input schemas after
  approval. Detecting it means starting the server and listing its tools,
  which would make the checker run the code it audits. Review the tool list
  whenever a server's pinned version changes.
### How does this relate to Agent Threat Rules (ATR)?

[ATR](https://github.com/Agent-Threat-Rule/agent-threat-rules) is an
MIT-licensed set of detection rules, mostly regular expressions, that match
attack content in prompts, tool calls and tool responses, with a scanner
that also reads skill and MCP files. This baseline is a set of pass/fail
configuration controls that the checker evaluates without model calls or
heuristics. The two answer different questions (is this content an attack, and
is this configuration safe to ship), so they are meant to run side by side.

### Are ATR rules part of this baseline?

No. A control is added only when it is a structural check on a configuration
artifact and cites an established source: an advisory, a CVE or a published
standard. Most ATR rules match exploit payloads for one product at run time,
which is out of scope here. ACB-MCP-003 is the one control derived from an
ATR rule (ATR-2026-02300); it cites the underlying OpenClaw advisory
(GHSA-mj59-h3q9-ghfh) and the VulnCheck record (CVE-2026-44995), not ATR
itself. The advisory says "No known CVE"; the CVE comes from VulnCheck only.

### Where do the mappings come from, and how do I check them?

Every OWASP, Five Eyes and NIST CSF ID in a control links to its source in
`docs/mappings.md` and on each control page. OWASP MCP Top 10 links point to
the entry files, Five Eyes and CSF links point to a PDF page, and OWASP AST
links point to the entry page. The OWASP Agentic Applications (ASI) links
point to the list page only, because it exposes no per-entry URLs, and ASI IDs
are not yet verified entry by entry. Only AST02 is verified (see
`docs/mappings.md`).

**CodeRabbit's findings hold up, and several let a cleartext or vulnerable declaration pass, so don't merge PR #50 yet.** CI is green, but my tests didn't cover these cases.

| Finding | Effect | Severity | How I checked |
|---|---|---|---|
| `mcp-proxy -- http://…` | TLS and auth checks skip the server | Missed failure | Reproduced |
| `mcp-proxy --verify-ssl true http://…` | `true` is read as the endpoint, so both checks skip | Missed failure | Reproduced |
| `mcp-remote@=0.1.15` | Vulnerable version passes MCP-004 | Missed failure | Reproduced; I didn't verify that npm accepts `=` |
| Two `--package=` options, `supergateway` first | `mcp-remote` is never checked for TLS, auth or version | Missed failure | Reproduced |
| `-p=mcp-remote@0.1.0` | The package and its version aren't recognised | Missed failure | Read from the code |
| `--header-file /etc/mcp-remote` | The filename is taken as the executable and the auth flag is lost | Wrong result | Reproduced |
| `mcp-remote mcp.example.com/mcp` (no scheme) | Skipped, though the procedure promises "not evaluated" | Missed finding | Reproduced |
| Version such as `0.1.0-beta \|\| 1.0.0` | A range is treated as an exact version | False failure | Read from the code |

The upstream behaviour for `--` and `--verify-ssl` comes from CodeRabbit's reading of `mcp-proxy` v0.10.0; I didn't open that source.

**Recommendation:** fix all eight, with a test for each. Most come from one design weakness: `proxy_launch` scans every word for a package name instead of separating runner options, the executable and the proxy's own arguments. I'd restructure it that way rather than add eight special cases. That is subtle enough that I'd switch to Opus with `/model opus` first.

| Finding | Effect | How I checked |
|---|---|---|
| `npx -c "supergateway<TAB>--sse<TAB>http://…"` | The call string isn't split without a literal space, so TLS and auth checks skip it | Read from the code |
| `mcp-remote … --header=Authorization:…` | Counts as authentication, but `mcp-remote` ignores that form | Matches the `main` source checked earlier; I didn't open v0.1.16 |
| `supergateway --header "X-Trace: 1" "Authorization: …"` | Only the first value is read, so a valid declaration fails auth | Code reads one value; upstream behaviour not verified |
| **Mine:** `docker run -v /a:/mcp-proxy …/mcp-proxy http://…` | The volume path is taken as the executable, so the cleartext URL is missed | Reproduced |

All four are worth fixing, with a test for each. The second matters most of the three from CodeRabbit, because it passes a server that may have no credential at all.

The Docker case shows a limit of the design: the parser still guesses which word is the executable when it doesn't know a runner option takes a value. For Docker, it should recognise the image only after consuming `docker run` options such as `-v`, `-e` and `--name`.

| Gap | Fix |
|---|---|
| Tab-separated `-c` string skipped | Every `-c`/`--call` value is now split, whatever the whitespace |

| Docker volume path taken as the executable | `docker run` options are consumed first, so the image is identified; `--entrypoint` is honoured |

**Also tightened:** for `mcp-remote` pinned at 0.1.16 or earlier, `--header-file`, `--client-metadata-url`, `--client-credentials` and `--device-code` no longer count as authentication, because 0.1.16 doesn't have them. - **`supergateway`:** reading several `--header` values rests on its `type: 'array'` definition and standard yargs behaviour; I didn't run it.
- **Design:** this parser will keep having edge cases, since it imitates five or so command-line parsers. I'd have the control text call it best-effort, and still get an Opus pass (`/model opus`) before merging.
